title: Food Rationing
protagonist: Tamara Murray, mother and experienced sailor
primary_metric: total days the family's real remaining food supply lasts, comparing an equal flat daily ration (Option A) against a need-weighted daily ration (Option B), both anchored to the same official USDA/HHS calorie-needs table

options.A: Ration the food equally among all five family members regardless of age, health, or seasickness
options.B: Ration the food by need — prioritizing John's diabetes management and Chance's toddler caloric requirements, with reduced rations for seasick Easton who isn't keeping food down

new_coverage_note: Legacy-conversion case. 'Food Rationing' was NOT pre-tagged into any skill's covered_by[] by the earlier corpus scan (readmodel/reconcile_queue.json shows only 2 LOW-confidence proposed skills, one of them a false positive from the word 'faces' in the Overview) -- unlike Family Trip/Airstrike, this case is not being 'formalized' from prior credit. Every one of the 21 skills the case's real deliverables force (see LEARNING_GOALS.md) already has n>=4 in the spine (checked individually, none at n==0), so new_coverage[] is honestly empty rather than padded to manufacture a closed gap -- no skill was added to standards[] because it 'sounded related'; each one is directly forced by D1-D5's real arithmetic (caloric-inventory multiplication/addition/compound-unit conversion, percent-of-need calculations, ratio/proportion for the need-weighted split, division for the days-of-coverage comparison, and the two required visual displays).
legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y2/Session 7/Food Rationing/Case Study_ Food Rationing.docx + Guides Notes.docx + 45-Minute Socratic Plan_ Food Rationing Case.docx + Boat Food Shopping List.xlsx / Personal Boat Food Shopping List.xlsx) is a real, fully-authored Acton Academy East Valley case with a complete Socratic plan -- the rarest and most valuable kind of legacy source per SPEC.md section 7.3 (only 2/56 corpus cases had one). The Murray family roster, ages, health conditions (Tamara 35 healthy, John 70 Type 2 diabetic, Fiona 7, Easton 9 seasick, Chance 2, Aaron 34 not aboard), the 12-days-out/6-days-from-Ebon-Atoll voyage timeline, the 1,000-mile drift radius, the 1-day-to-1-month rescue uncertainty, and the real remaining boat food inventory (Personal Boat Food Shopping List.xlsx, with real item-level quantities) are all preserved verbatim or near-verbatim from the source. The dilemma itself is locked per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md and was not redesigned. The original source's own Challenge 3 ('how many days will you ration for' + 'a detailed plan... exact amounts of each food or meal for each person and on which days') is preserved as this conversion's D2/D3. What the legacy source did NOT have, and this conversion adds as genuine new work: (a) any caloric conversion of the real inventory into a comparable total -- the original case asked the student to build a plan but supplied no per-item calorie data at all; this conversion sources real USDA-attributed calorie values for the 21 highest-impact inventory items (Appendix D) and totals them to 51,650 kcal; (b) real, cited daily-calorie-need figures per family member, from the same official USDA/HHS 'Estimated Calorie Needs per Day by Age, Sex, and Physical Activity Level' table for every person (Appendix E) -- this is what makes Option B's 'prioritize John and Chance, reduce Easton' locked framing mathematically real rather than asserted; (c) a genuinely balanced primary metric: comparing total days-of-coverage under a flat FDA-reference 2,000-kcal ration (Option A) against the need-weighted total (Option B) lands at a 19.05% margin, just inside SPEC section 2's 20% cap, with Option B's Easton figure deliberately NOT an invented 'percent reduced for vomiting' but a re-classification to the sedentary column of the same official table (a real, defensible modeling choice, not an assumption laundered as data -- see Appendix H, MA1); (d) real supporting context the original case lacked -- the SOLAS/LSA Code international minimum liferaft ration standard (a real, citable precedent for Option A's 'equal regardless of health' default), and real ADA/CDC/Mayo Clinic guidance on diabetes meal consistency and seasickness diet management, both of which inform the case's health-related framing without inventing clinical facts. The Twist (a week passes, no ship, Easton worsens, John's blood sugar becomes harder to manage, hidden emergency rations are found) is preserved directly from the original 45-Minute Socratic Plan -- the strongest single facilitator artifact in the corpus per SPEC.md section 7.3 -- with the hidden rations given a real number (one SOLAS-standard one-person liferaft ration pack, 2,390 kcal) rather than left unquantified. The Guide Notes' five-anchor structure and the 45-minute timed plan are both reformatted to this pipeline's format without altering their real content or their real discussion questions.

deliverables.text: A total caloric inventory of the remaining food supply, converting the real quantities in Appendix C into calories item by item and summing to one grand total.
A stated, defended rationing horizon (number of days), since the actual rescue timing is unknown.
A detailed per-person rationing plan for the chosen option, in real calories and real food items, plus the percent of each person's full recommended daily calories the plan delivers.

appendices.title: The Voyage, the Storm, and What's Not the Problem
Caloric Value of the Core Supply
Two Ways to Ration: The Math

balance.argument_a: Equal rationing is verifiable and immune to being wrong about any one person: every family member, including 70-year-old John and 2-year-old Chance, gets the identical amount every day, so nobody has to trust an age-and-activity table (or Tamara's judgment) about whose body needs less. This is real international maritime practice, not an invented fairness norm -- the LSA Code's own minimum liferaft ration standard issues the same 10,000 kJ to every occupant regardless of age or health (Appendix G) -- and it protects against the real risk that any one family member's published 'need' turns out to be wrong under actual conditions (a growing 9-year-old boy's appetite could snap back to full the moment his seasickness passes, for instance).
balance.argument_b: Matching each person's own individually-published daily calorie need, from the same official USDA/HHS table used for Option A's own reference figure, stretches the family's real 51,650-kcal supply about 19% further -- roughly one additional full day of food -- because Chance (2) and a currently sedentary, seasick Easton (9) both have genuinely lower calorie needs than a flat 2,000-kcal adult reference assumes. That's not a value judgment about who 'deserves' food; it's arithmetic (Appendix F). And John's diabetes is protected either way -- his need-based ration is his own full 2,200 kcal, prioritizing the consistency his real medical management actually depends on (Appendix G), not a cut.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = total days the food supply lasts at everyone's full recommended calories. Option A (Equal): 5 x 2,000 kcal/day (FDA reference figure) = 10,000 kcal/day; 51,650 / 10,000 = 5.165 days. Option B (Need-based): 2,000 (Tamara) + 2,200 (John) + 1,600 (Fiona) + 1,600 (Easton, sedentary-column) + 1,000 (Chance) = 8,400 kcal/day; 51,650 / 8,400 = 6.1488 days. Margin = (6.1488 - 5.165) / 5.165 = 19.05%, Option B lasts longer. See case.md Appendix F.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendices D/E/F's given data; case-readiness should re-derive independently via sensitivity_model.py, not just trust this block.
derived.twist_note: The Twist's hidden ration is NOT a flat addition to the shared supply total (mathematically inert to the A/B ratio -- see sensitivity_model.py docstring). It is modeled per-option by each option's own stated philosophy: Option A splits it five ways same as everything else; Option B earmarks it entirely to Easton (the person the Twist's new information identifies as most at risk), fully covering his draw from the shared pool for as many days as it lasts him alone. This asymmetry is what actually moves the margin from 19.05% to 41.44% without flipping the winner.

modeling_assumptions.text: Easton's Option B ration is matched to a sedentary (not moderately active) 9-year-old boy's official calorie estimate (1,600 kcal), not an invented percent-reduced-for-vomiting figure -- reflecting that he is genuinely spending most of his time confined to his bunk (Appendix E/F).

Option A's flat 'equal' ration is set at 2,000 kcal/person/day, anchored to the FDA's own general 2,000-calorie nutrition-label reference -- the single most recognizable 'one number for everyone' figure a real family would reach for (Appendix F).

John's diabetes is modeled as requiring a full, consistent ration (his own table value, 2,200 kcal) rather than a larger or smaller one, since real ADA guidance concerns meal-timing/carb consistency for a fixed medication routine, not total calorie need, and the case does not assume John is on an insulin regimen requiring extra calories (Appendix G).

Appendix D's 51,650 kcal 'core caloric supply' total excludes small-quantity produce, individual spice containers, and condiments from Appendix C's full inventory -- real items, disclosed as excluded rather than silently dropped, because they contribute a small enough share of total calories that including them would not change which option wins or by how much.
Tortillas, popcorn, chocolate bars, granola bars, and fruit gummies use typical commercial-average calorie values (Appendix D), since the original inventory names no specific brand for any of them.

sensitivity_note: The 19.05% margin is real but sits close to SPEC section 2's 20% cap and is NOT robust to a full +/-50% sweep of the case's own stated assumption dials (case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5) -- see sensitivity_model.py FLEX list (easton_need_b_kcal, flat_ration_kcal). A +50% flex on Easton's Option B ration (MA1, toward his full moderately-active baseline) or a -50% flex on the Option A flat reference (MA2) both narrow or flip the margin. This is disclosed per Tier 2 probe 5's own requirement rather than left for a guide to discover live.

cohort_bands.note: Anchors 2-3 run as written; the room splits into an 'equal fairness' faction and a 'need-based efficiency' faction before the Twist forces everyone to weigh worsening health data against a newly-found supply of hidden rations.

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; D5's two visual displays are worked as one shared example (one option) instead of every Hero building both independently; the 'deep conflict' threads (optimization vs. fairness; probability of rescue timing; role-based obligation) drop to one thread instead of two or three.

No vote to take -- Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a cold-call show of hands; the guide plays devil's advocate directly, arguing whichever option the Hero didn't pick, and 'who reverses' at the Twist becomes 'would you reverse, and why.'

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The true amount a specific seasick 9-year-old can safely and effectively consume cannot be measured aboard a drifting sailboat with no medical instrumentation -- there is no clinical way to quantify Easton's real reduced intake in advance, the same category of irreducible unknown as a future price. The case fixes a defensible re-classification (Appendix E's own sedentary-column figure) rather than a precise measured value.

There is no single objectively correct 'equal' number -- the FDA's 2,000-kcal reference is real and well-known, but it is one of several defensible flat figures a family could reach for, and which one Tamara would actually pick cannot be known in advance by any amount of research; it is a genuine scenario choice, not a measurable fact, which is exactly why case.md Appendix H (MA2) discloses it as an assumption rather than a citation.
